content.narrative_summary: This page continues a discussion of diameter thresholds for ascending aorta dilatation and aneurysm based on clinical studies. Borger et al studied patients with bicuspid aortic valve undergoing AVR and found that baseline diameters of 4.5–4.9 cm carried a significantly increased risk of aneurysm, dissection, or death compared with diameters <4.5 cm. Paruchuri et al analyzed MESA data and reported that a 4.0–4.4 cm diameter conferred an 89-fold relative increase in dissection risk and ≥4.5 cm conferred a 6,000-fold increase, justifying definitions of “dilated” (≥4.0 cm) and “aneurysm” (≥4.5 cm). Only 2.6% of the cohort met the dilated threshold and 0.2% met the aneurysm threshold. The definition aligns with 2014 ESC guidelines, and “dilation” is preferred over “ectasia.”

content.narrative_summary: The page describes mechanisms of static, dynamic, and combined obstruction in aortic dissection (illustrated in Figure 9) due to true and false lumen interactions. content.title: 3. IMAGING AND MEASUREMENTS
section_headings: 3.1. Aortic Imaging Techniques to Determine Presence and Progression of Aortic Disease
content.narrative_summary: The page provides a synopsis highlighting the roles of CT, MRI, TTE, TEE, and abdominal ultrasound in optimized depiction of aortic anatomy, noting modality selection based on patient-specific factors (hemodynamic stability, contrast allergy, renal function, tolerance), and the growing use of high-resolution 3D imaging supplanting catheter angiography. It then begins recommendation-specific supportive text advising that measurements be obtained perpendicular to the aortic long axis at specified locations with multiplanar reformats created on 3D datasets.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Aortic Imaging Techniques to Determine Presence and Progression of Aortic Disease

rows.recommendation: In patients with known or suspected aortic disease, aortic diameters should be measured at reproducible anatomic landmarks perpendicular to axis of blood flow, and these measurement methods should be reported in a clear and consistent manner. In cases of asymmetric or oval contour, the longest diameter and its perpendicular diameter should be reported.3,4
In patients with known or suspected aortic disease, episodic and cumulative ionizing radiation doses should be kept as low as feasible while maintaining diagnostic image quality.5-7

In patients with known or suspected aortic disease, when performing CT or MR imaging, it is recommended that the root and ascending aortic diameters be measured from inner-edge to inner-edge, using an electrocardiographic-synchronized technique. If there are aortic wall abnormalities, such as atherosclerosis or discrete wall thickening (more common in the distal aorta), the outer-edge to outer-edge diameter should be reported (Table 4).

In patients with known or suspected aortic disease, the aortic root diameter should be recorded as maximum sinus to sinus measurement. In the setting of known asymmetry, multiple measurements should be reported, and both short- and long-axis images of the root should be obtained to avoid underestimation of the diameter.
In patients with known or suspected aortic disease, it is reasonable that a dilated root or ascending aorta be indexed to patient height or BSA in the report, to aid in clinical risk assessment.8-11
In patients with known or suspected aortic disease, when performing echocardiography, it is reasonable to measure the aorta from leading-edge to leading-edge, perpendicular to the axis of blood flow.
Using inner-edge to inner-edge measurements may also be considered, particularly on short-axis imaging.

content.title: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline
content.narrative_summary: This page discusses noninvasive imaging modalities for aortic disease. Under section 3.2.1, it describes computed tomography (CT), including use of electrocardiographic-gated techniques to reduce motion artifact, contrast and noncontrast imaging, risks of iodinated contrast in renal impairment, sensitivity and specificity for acute aortic syndromes, and CT angiography protocols. Section 3.2.2 covers magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), highlighting coverage of the aorta and branch vessels, physiologic assessment of ventricular and valve function, advantages (no ionizing radiation, precise 3D datasets), limitations (artifacts, availability, contraindications, longer acquisition), MRA techniques including gadolinium-based contrast risks, and noncontrast sequences. Section 3.2.3 introduces transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) as the primary nonemergency imaging for the thoracic aorta, its utility for aortic root and valve assessment, visualization of arch branch vessels, portability, and use in surveillance and complication detection.

content.narrative_summary: The page discusses imaging modalities for aortic disease: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) provides high-resolution images of the thoracic aorta and aortic valve anatomy/function, useful intraoperatively and for guiding operative and endovascular repair. Intravascular ultrasound offers high-resolution intraluminal imaging to assess aortic size, tortuosity, plaque, calcification, branch vessels, and distinguish true and false lumens, guiding endovascular stent deployment and reducing contrast. Abdominal ultrasound is recommended for screening and surveillance of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) using outer-edge measurements (>3.0 cm), with B-mode, Doppler, and spectral analysis detecting aneurysms, thrombus, dissection, and endoleaks post-EVAR, though limitations include interobserver variability and obesity. The page then introduces multidisciplinary aortic teams.

content.narrative_summary: The page presents Figure 15, illustrating that both actual mortality and the ratio of actual to predicted mortality (A/P ratio) decrease as annual center case volume increases (>20–25 cases and further at >50 cases). The narrative discusses that multidisciplinary thoracic aortic programs are associated with significant mortality reductions compared to hospitals without such programs. A Medicare study of 230,736 patients showed adjusted mortality decreasing with higher hospital procedural volume, notably for open repair. Hughes et al. found a negative association between hospital volume and mortality in >13,000 elective aortic procedures, especially below 30–40 cases/year. Mori et al.’s contemporary series of >53,000 thoracic aortic surgeries confirmed lower operative mortality at volumes >20–25 and >50 cases/year. Among 232 acute type A dissections in the UK, expert aortic surgeons had lower 30-day mortality (10% vs 26%), performed root procedures more often with shorter cross-clamp times, and acute dissection repair mortality was 14% vs 24% for high- vs low-volume surgeons. The guideline emphasizes referral to high-volume centers and multidisciplinary teams for complex aortic interventions.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Shared Decision-Making

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with aortic disease, shared decision-making is recommended when determining the appropriate thresholds for intervention, deciding on the type of surgical repair, choosing between open surgical versus endovascular approaches; and in medical management and surveillance.

2. In patients with aortic disease who are contemplating pregnancy or who are pregnant, shared decision-making is recommended when considering the cardiovascular risks of pregnancy, the diameter thresholds for prophylactic aortic surgery, and the mode of delivery.

content.narrative_summary: Approximately 20% of thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAAs) are related to heritable thoracic aortic disease (HTAD), including syndromic forms with multisystem features and nonsyndromic familial TAA (FTAA). Syndromic HTAD most commonly involves the aortic root and ascending aorta but may extend distally. Pathogenic variants in multiple genes can lead to TAA, cerebral aneurysms, and abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). Up to 20% of individuals with a TAA or aortic dissection have a family history, and population studies show a significantly increased risk of TAA and dissection in first-degree relatives. Screening of asymptomatic first-degree relatives with imaging is essential to detect unrecognized thoracic aortic disease.

section_headings: 6.1.2.1. HTAD: Genetic Testing and Screening of Family Members for TAD
content.narrative_summary: This section contrasts sporadic aneurysms of the aortic root and ascending aorta with those of the descending thoracic aorta, noting differences in age at diagnosis (younger for root/ascending vs older for descending), lower prevalence of traditional atherosclerotic risk factors and aortic calcification in sporadic proximal aneurysms, and differing etiologies (congenital/hereditary vs atherosclerotic). It references further discussion of medical, surgical, and endovascular management in later sections. It then introduces genetic aortopathies and the specific topic of HTAD genetic testing and family screening.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for HTAD: Genetic Testing and Screening of Family Members for TAD

rows.recommendation: In patients with aortic root/ascending aortic aneurysms or aortic dissection, obtaining a multigenerational family history of TAD, unexplained sudden deaths, and peripheral and intracranial aneurysms is recommended.

In patients with aortic root/ascending aortic aneurysms or aortic dissection and risk factors for HTAD (Table 8, Figure 17), genetic testing to identify pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants (ie, mutations) is recommended.

In patients with an established pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in a gene predisposing to HTAD, it is recommended that genetic counseling be provided and the patient's clinical management be informed by the specific gene and variant in the gene.

In patients with TAD who have a pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant, genetic testing of at-risk biological relatives (ie, cascade testing) is recommended. In family members who are found by genetic screening to have inherited the pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant, aortic imaging with TTE (if aortic root and ascending aorta are adequately visualized, otherwise with CT or MRI) is recommended.

In a family with aortic root/ascending aortic aneurysms or aortic dissection, if the disease-causing variant is not identified with genetic testing, screening aortic imaging (as per recommendation 4) of at-risk biological relatives (ie, cascade testing) is recommended.

In patients with aortic root/ascending aortic aneurysms or aortic dissection, in the absence of either a known family history of TAD or pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant, screening aortic imaging (as per recommendation 4) of first-degree relatives is recommended.

In patients with acute type A aortic dissection, the diameter of the aortic root and ascending aorta should be recorded in the operative note and medical record to inform the management of affected relatives.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes that pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in genes predispose to thoracic aortic disease (TAD), recommending multigene panel testing for hereditary TAD (HTAD) and cascade testing of at-risk relatives. Supportive text notes that 13%–20% of TAD patients without syndromic features have similarly affected first-degree relatives, that inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance and expression, and that genetic testing panels include 11 highly penetrant genes. Variants of uncertain significance should not guide management. Specific gene mutations confer varied risks for aortic and vascular disease presentations, and genetic counseling is integral for risk assessment and family testing.

content.title: Figure 17 Evaluation and Genetic Testing Protocol for Patients With TAD
content.narrative_summary: Caption describes that genetic testing is recommended for individuals with syndromic features (MFS, LDS, vEDS), family history of TAD or aneurysm, and/or early age of onset. Thoracic imaging is advised for first-degree relatives to detect asymptomatic aneurysms. Positive genetic results trigger gene-based management and cascade testing of at-risk relatives. Negative or VUS results lead to imaging of relatives for aortic dilation. Footnotes define abbreviations and note that aneurysms are typically asymptomatic.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Figure 17
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Evaluation and Genetic Testing Protocol for Patients With TAD
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
Flowchart outlining evaluation and genetic testing protocol for patients with thoracic aortic disease:
– Entry criteria: features of MFS, LDS, or vEDS; family history of TAD, intracranial or peripheral aneurysm; TAD < 60 y; or sporadic patients ≥ 60 y.
– Sporadic patients ≥ 60 y with at-risk family undergo imaging; if aortic dilation/aneurysm detected, proceed as below; if normal, no further action.
– Patients meeting entry criteria undergo genetic testing.
– Positive (pathogenic/likely pathogenic) results lead to cascade testing of at-risk relatives and gene-based management; relatives testing positive are managed as offspring.
– Negative or VUS results prompt imaging for aortic dilation/aneurysm in at-risk family members; relatives testing negative are considered at general population risk for TAAD.

section_headings: 6.1.2.1.1. Surgical Considerations for Nonsyndromic Heritable TAAs and No Identified Genetic Cause
content.narrative_summary: Paragraphs 4 through 7 emphasize the role of cascade screening with aortic imaging for asymptomatic family members carrying pathogenic HTAD variants or with a family history of thoracic aortic dissection (TAD). They note that even in the absence of identified pathogenic variants, screening should be considered, with repeat imaging intervals guided by age and family history. The text highlights that surveillance is best directed by family history, that there is no upper age limit for imaging, and that specific aortic diameters at dissection or repair should be recorded in the medical record to inform management of affected relatives.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Surgical Considerations for Nonsyndromic Heritable TAA and No Identified Genetic Cause

rows.recommendation: 1. In asymptomatic patients with aneurysms of the aortic root or ascending aorta with nonsyndromic heritable thoracic aortic disease (nsHTAD) and no identified genetic cause, determining the timing of surgical repair requires shared decision-making and is informed by known aortic diameters at the time of aortic dissection, TAA repair, or both in affected family members.1-4

2. In asymptomatic patients with aneurysms of the aortic root or ascending aorta with nsHTAD and no identified genetic cause but no information on aortic diameters at the time of dissection or aneurysm repair in affected family members and who have no high-risk features for adverse aortic events (Table 9) it is recommended to repair the aorta when the maximal diameter reaches ≥5.0 cm.1

3. In patients with aneurysms of the aortic root or ascending aorta with nsHTAD and no identified genetic cause and a maximal aortic diameter of ≥4.5 cm, who have high-risk features for adverse aortic events (Table 9), or who are undergoing cardiac surgery for other indications, aortic repair is reasonable when performed by experienced surgeons in a Multidisciplinary Aortic Team.5

section_headings: 6.1.2.2.1 Diagnostic and Surveillance Aortic Imaging in Marfan Syndrome
content.narrative_summary: This page presents recommendations for diagnostic and surveillance aortic imaging in patients with Marfan syndrome, followed by a synopsis of Marfan syndrome’s genetic basis and pathophysiology. It also begins the recommendation-specific supportive text describing the leading causes of morbidity in Marfan syndrome.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnostic and Surveillance Aortic Imaging in Marfan Syndrome

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with Marfan syndrome, a TTE is recommended at the time of initial diagnosis, to determine the diameters of the aortic root and ascending aorta, and 6 months thereafter, to determine the rate of aortic growth; if the aortic diameters are stable, an annual surveillance TTE is recommended.1 If the aortic root, ascending aorta, or both are not adequately visualized on TTE, a CT or MRI of the thoracic aorta is recommended.2
2. In adults with Marfan syndrome, after the initial TTE, a CT or MRI of the thoracic aorta is reasonable to confirm the aortic diameters and assess the remainder of the thoracic aorta.

3. In patients with Marfan syndrome who have undergone aortic root replacement, surveillance imaging of the thoracic aorta by MRI (or CT) is recommended to evaluate for distal TAD, initially annually and then, if normal in diameter and unchanged after 2 years, every other year.3-6
4. In patients with Marfan syndrome who have undergone aortic root replacement, surveillance imaging every 3 to 5 years for potential AAA is reasonable.2,6

section_headings: 6.1.2.2.3. Marfan Syndrome Interventions: Replacement of the Aortic Root in Patients With Marfan Syndrome
content.narrative_summary: Continuation of discussion on Marfan syndrome management: patients may develop disease of the descending aorta. Thorough TTE can assess aortic root, ascending aorta, aortic arch, proximal and distal descending aorta; CT or MRI may be used for distal segments not well visualized on TTE. Surgical aortic root replacement prevents type A dissection and improves longevity. Long-term complications after root replacement include graft infections, pseudoaneurysms, distal aneurysms, and distal aortic dissection. Distal thoracic and abdominal aneurysms occur less commonly but are seen in those with prior root replacement or smoking.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Medical Therapy in Marfan Syndrome

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with Marfan syndrome, treatment with either a beta blocker or an ARB, in maximally tolerated doses (unless contraindicated), is recommended to reduce the rate of aortic dilation.1,2
2. In patients with Marfan syndrome, the use of both a beta blocker and an ARB, in maximally tolerated doses (unless contraindicated), is reasonable to reduce the rate of aortic dilation.3,4

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes that prophylactic aortic root replacement in Marfan syndrome prevents type A dissection and improves survival, with surgical thresholds influenced by patient age, body size, family history, and aortic growth rate. rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with Turner syndrome, TTE and cardiac MRI are recommended at the time of diagnosis to evaluate for BAV, aortic root and ascending aortic dilation, aortic coarctation, and other congenital heart defects.1–9

2. In patients with Turner syndrome who are ≥15 years old, the use of the ASI (ratio of aortic diameter [cm] to BSA [m2]) is recommended to define the degree of aortic dilation and assess the risk of aortic dissection.9,10,11

3. In patients with Turner syndrome without risk factors for aortic dissection (Table 12), surveillance imaging with TTE or MRI to evaluate the aorta is recommended every 5 years in children and every 10 years in adults, as well as before planning a pregnancy.9,10,11
4. In patients with Turner syndrome and an ASI >2.3 cm/m2, surveillance imaging of the aorta is recommended at least annually.9

5. In patients with Turner syndrome and risk factors for aortic dissection (Table 12), surveillance aortic imaging at an interval depending on the aortic diameter, ASI, and aortic growth rate is recommended (Figure 18).9

6a. In patients with Turner syndrome who are ≥15 years old and have an ASI of ≥2.5 cm/m2 plus risk factors for aortic dissection (Table 12), surgical intervention to replace the aortic root, ascending aorta, or both is reasonable.9,10
6b. In those without risk factors for aortic dissection, surgical intervention to replace the aortic root, ascending aorta, or both may be considered.

content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: The goal of blood pressure (BP) control in thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is to slow growth and prevent aortic dissection and nonaortic cardiovascular events. An SBP goal of ≤130 mm Hg and DBP goal of ≤80 mm Hg using antihypertensive therapy is advised; more intensive SBP targets (<120 mm Hg) may benefit selected patients if tolerated. Limited data exist on beta-blocker and ARB therapy in TAA, with most robust evidence from Marfan syndrome cohorts (see Section 6.1.2.2, “Marfan Syndrome”). Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text: No randomized trials have defined optimal BP thresholds in TAA; ACC/AHA guidelines recommend SBP <130 mm Hg and DBP <80 mm Hg. The SPRINT trial showed intensive BP control to SBP <120 mm Hg reduced cardiovascular events by 25% and all-cause mortality by 27%. Prospective data on beta-blockers are limited but suggest slowed aortic growth in Marfan syndrome. Meta-analysis of ARBs in Marfan syndrome showed slower aortic root growth versus placebo and beta-blockers; combination therapy may be superior. A Japanese antihypertensive regimen including valsartan lowered adverse cardiovascular events, but the study was retracted and LOE downgraded from B to C.

section_headings: 6.5. Surgical and Endovascular Management of Aortic Aneurysms
6.5.1. Surgery for Sporadic Aneurysms of the Aortic Root and Ascending Aorta
content.narrative_summary: This section explains that most patients with thoracic (TAA) and abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are asymptomatic, and that surgical or endovascular intervention aims to reduce adverse aortic events—dissection, rupture, or aortic-related death—by balancing anatomic assessment against procedural risk. Open surgery involves replacing the aneurysmal segment with a prosthetic graft anastomosed to nonaneurysmal tissue while preserving branch vessels. Endovascular repair uses contiguous aortic or iliac segments to fix stent grafts and exclude flow from the aneurysm sac. The FDA has approved stent grafts for descending thoracic, juxtarenal, and infrarenal segments; devices for ascending aorta and arch are investigational. Long-term surveillance after endovascular repair is necessary due to risks of aneurysm sac enlargement outside trial criteria.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Surgery for Sporadic Aneurysms of the Aortic Root and Ascending Aorta

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with aneurysms of the aortic root and ascending aorta who have symptoms attributable to the aneurysm, surgery is indicated.1,2
2. In asymptomatic patients with aneurysms of the aortic root or ascending aorta who have a maximum diameter of ≥5.5 cm, surgery is indicated.3–9

3. In patients with an aneurysm of the aortic root or ascending aorta of <5.5 cm, whose growth rate confirmed by tomographic imaging is ≥0.3 cm/y in 2 consecutive years, or ≥0.5 cm in 1 year, surgery is indicated.10–13

4. In asymptomatic patients with aneurysms of the aortic root or ascending aorta who have a maximum diameter of ≥5.0 cm, surgery is reasonable when performed by experienced surgeons in a Multidisciplinary Aortic Team.14–17

5. In patients undergoing repair or replacement of a tricuspid aortic valve who have a concomitant aneurysm of the ascending aorta with a maximum diameter of ≥4.5 cm, ascending aortic replacement is reasonable when performed by experienced surgeons in a Multidisciplinary Aortic Team.18–21

In patients undergoing repair or replacement of a tricuspid aortic valve who have a concomitant aneurysm of the ascending aorta with a maximum diameter of ≥5.0 cm, ascending aortic replacement is reasonable.18–21

In patients undergoing cardiac surgery for indications other than aortic valve repair or replacement who have a concomitant aneurysm of ascending aorta with a maximum diameter of ≥5.0 cm, ascending aortic replacement may be reasonable.18

6. In patients with a height >1 standard deviation above or below the mean who have an asymptomatic aneurysm of the aortic root or ascending aorta and a maximal cross-sectional aortic area/height ratio of ≥10 cm2/m, surgery is reasonable when performed by experienced surgeons in a Multidisciplinary Aortic Team.14,15,22

7. In asymptomatic patients with aneurysms of the aortic root or ascending aorta who have either an ASI of ≥3.08 cm/m2 or AHI of ≥3.21 cm/m, surgery may be reasonable when performed by experienced surgeons in a Multidisciplinary Aortic Team.23

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis discusses the timing of elective surgery for aneurysms of the aortic root and ascending aorta, emphasizing that surgery is indicated when the risk of dissection, rupture, or sudden death outweighs operative risk. It notes the lack of prospective studies evaluating various aortic size and wall stress parameters, describes the mechanical basis for rupture and dissection, and reviews the historical 5.5 cm diameter threshold. The recommendation-specific supportive text elaborates on: 1) symptomatic compression and pain signaling rupture risk; 2) the 5.5 cm diameter criterion, operative mortality, and factors affecting risk; 3) variability in growth rates—especially in patients with tricuspid valves—and measurement challenges; 4) the correlation of dissection risk with larger diameters and growth rates, including data showing dramatically increased risk at sizes ≥4 cm; and 5) considerations for concomitant aneurysm repair during aortic valve surgery.

content.narrative_summary: This section continues the discussion on aortic root replacement, emphasizing individualized decision‐making based on aneurysm size, valve repair versus replacement options, patient factors, and comorbidities. IRAD data demonstrate that many dissections occur at diameters below 5.5 cm, highlighting the limitations of absolute diameter as a risk predictor and the potential value of indexed measures (aortic area‐to‐height, diameter‐to‐BSA or height) and biomechanical parameters. A large single‐center database reindexed diameters to BSA and height, and cross‐sectional aortic area to height ratio was found to predict mortality in unoperated patients with root or ascending aneurysms (tricuspid or bicuspid). Multidisciplinary teams may consider such indexed thresholds—particularly in women—for optimal timing of prophylactic repair, though prospective validation is needed.

content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis reviews comparative outcomes of thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) versus open surgical repair for descending thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA). Early trials demonstrated reduced perioperative morbidity, shorter hospital stay, and lower aneurysm-related mortality with TEVAR, but Medicare data show that the perioperative advantage is lost by 1 year with worse 5-year survival after TEVAR versus open repair (79% vs 89%). Outcomes also vary by institutional volume and patient factors (e.g., connective tissue disorders or life expectancy). The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text details key clinical device trial findings: 5-year aneurysm mortality reduction, adverse event and reintervention rates, and comparative outcomes of TEVAR versus open repair at 30 days and 1 year; access complications related to device delivery; and volume-related mortality differences from registry and Medicare Provider Analysis data, supporting individualized decision-making based on anatomy, access, and patient life expectancy.

The page presents guidance on management of the left subclavian and celiac arteries in descending thoracic aortic (TAA) TEVAR. Left subclavian artery coverage is required in up to 40% of cases; preoperative revascularization is recommended to prevent spinal cord injury (SCI) and may reduce stroke risk and other ischemic complications. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency, left arm ischemia, and preservation of preexisting internal mammary grafts or dialysis access inform revascularization decisions. Celiac artery coverage is needed in about 15% of TEVAR cases; despite low incidence of postoperative visceral ischemia, preoperative confirmation of adequate collateralization with CTA, angiography, or both is reasonable.

content.narrative_summary: Iliac artery access for stent-graft delivery in descending thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is marginal in up to 21% of cases, requiring careful preoperative CTA review. Marginal or inadequate access can be managed with surgical bypass, direct aortic or iliac exposure, iliac conduits, or endovascular techniques. Percutaneous femoral access has been applied safely with high technical success (94.4–98.9%), fewer complications, and shorter hospital stay compared to open cutdown. In clinical trials, alternative access was required in 9.4–21.1% of patients with small or diseased vessels.

3. In patients with descending TAA undergoing TEVAR who have suitable anatomy, total percutaneous femoral access is a reasonable alternative to open surgical cutdown to avoid access-related complications.

content.narrative_summary:
Synopsis: No randomized controlled trials compare early or late outcomes of open versus endovascular repair of thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysms (TAAA). As of November 2022, no FDA-approved endovascular devices exist; current procedures use customized fenestrated or branched devices under investigational or industry-sponsored trials. Open repair remains the preferred therapy with excellent results in high-volume centers (operative mortality ~7.5% in 3,309 patients; low aortic‐related reintervention rates; spinal cord ischemia [SCI] risk ~2%), and other centers report similar outcomes.  
Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text: 1) In ruptured TAAA, open repair by multidisciplinary teams can achieve low mortality (14%) and SCI rates (5%), with 5-year survival ~47.5%; registry data show 10% mortality but high stroke (14.7%), SCI (9.6%), and reintervention (19.7%) rates with 5-year survival ~31.9%. 2) Endovascular repair is limited by patient instability, custom graft lead time, and small published series; off-the-shelf branched devices may be considered in selected hemodynamically stable, high-risk cases (symptomatic/contained rupture) with reported 15% mortality for symptomatic and 30% for ruptured TAAA. 3) In known/suspected connective tissue disorders (e.g., Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, Ehlers-Danlos syndromes), open repair is recommended due to lower operative mortality and excellent long-term freedom from reintervention; small series of fenestrated-branched endovascular repair report 0% mortality, 100% technical success, and one reintervention over 34 months. 4) Investigational fenestrated and branched endovascular stent graft trials show promising technical success (92%–99.6%), low perioperative mortality, branch vessel patency 96%–98% at 1 year, 91% freedom from aortic-related death, and 57% overall survival at 3 years.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes spinal cord injury (SCI) as a significant complication of open and endovascular thoracoabdominal aneurysm repair, with incidence ranging from 2% to 15% influenced by aneurysm extent, patient comorbidities, urgency, and surgical experience. It reviews prior guidelines and randomized data supporting cerebrospinal fluid drainage and outlines other adjunctive measures (volume loading, blood pressure augmentation, oxygen delivery). The recommendation-specific text emphasizes the formidable nature of TAAA repair, the potential for temporary or permanent SCI, various intraoperative techniques, and institutional practices (hypothermic arrest, clamp-and-sew, neuromonitoring), noting that cerebrospinal fluid drainage remains the only proven perioperative protective technique. It begins discussion of delayed paraplegia incidence, which continues onto the next page.

2. In patients who experience delayed spinal cord dysfunction after either open or endovascular TAAA repair, timely measures to optimize spinal cord perfusion and decrease intrathecal pressure are recommended (Table 20).¹⁻⁴,⁸

content.title: 6.5.5.3. Threshold for AAA Repair
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis discusses that maximum aneurysm diameter is the primary risk factor for AAA growth and rupture. Historical trials of early repair for aneurysms 4.0–5.4 cm showed no survival benefit but higher reintervention rates. Rupture risk thresholds differ for women, who tend to rupture at smaller diameters, and aortic indexing (aneurysm size/BSA) may better predict rupture than diameter alone. Limited data on saccular AAAs suggest morphologic features influence rupture risk. Ongoing research is needed to refine repair thresholds and metrics such as ASI versus maximum diameter.

In patients with unruptured saccular AAA, intervention to reduce the risk of rupture may be reasonable.
In patients with unruptured AAA and aneurysm growth of ≥0.5 cm in 6 months, repair to reduce the risk of rupture may be reasonable.

section_headings: 6.5.5.4. Open Versus Endovascular Repair of AAA
content.narrative_summary:
Observational studies indicate that symptomatic AAAs carry higher mortality and morbidity than those managed electively, though timing of repair remains controversial; optimizing cardiorespiratory status during nonemergent surgery may be beneficial. Saccular AAAs are uncommon (6.1% of AAA cases in one registry), more frequent in women, and often symptomatic at smaller diameters (25% ≥5.5 cm; 8.4% <4.5 cm). Aneurysm growth rates vary by size (1.5–2 mm/y for 3.0–3.9 cm; 3.3–5.7 mm/y for 4.0–5.9 cm), and increases ≥0.5 cm in 6 months or ≥1 cm in 1 year denote rapid growth warranting consideration of repair. Four major trials excluded rapidly growing AAAs (≥7 mm in 6 months or >10 mm in 12 months).

The range of AAA repair options has expanded substantially since 1952, particularly with EVAR enabling treatment of patients ineligible for open surgery due to comorbidities. Early RCTs showed an initial survival advantage for EVAR that dissipates over time; more recent data demonstrate sustained perioperative survival benefits but with diminishing long-term differences.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Open Versus Endovascular Repair of AAA

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with nonruptured AAA with low to moderate operative risk and who have anatomy suitable for either open or EVAR, a shared decision-making process weighing the risks and benefits of each approach is recommended.1-11
2. In patients undergoing elective endovascular repair for nonruptured AAA, adherence to manufacturer's instructions for use is recommended.12-16
3. In patients with nonruptured AAA and a high perioperative risk, EVAR is reasonable to reduce the risk of 30-day morbidity, mortality, or both.9,10

4. For patients with nonruptured AAA, a moderate to high perioperative risk, and anatomy suitable for an FDA-approved fenestrated endovascular device, endovascular repair is reasonable over open repair to reduce the risk of perioperative complications.10,11,17,18

content.narrative_summary: This section provides supportive evidence for endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) versus open surgery for infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). Pooled RCT data show lower perioperative mortality for EVAR (OR 0.36; 95% CI, 0.2–0.66) through 6 months, with equivalent survival thereafter but higher long-term aneurysm-related death and reintervention rates (hazard ratio 5.12; 95% CI, 1.6–16.4; OR for rupture 5; death attributable to rupture OR 3.6). Observational Medicare studies confirm longer-term survival advantages in certain groups. Deviations from device instructions increase graft migration, endoleaks, rupture, and mortality (hazard ratio 1.2; 95% CI, 1.02–1.42). The EVAR-2 trial in high-risk patients initially showed no survival benefit but later demonstrated lower aneurysm-related mortality (hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI, 0.34–0.91). EVAR perioperative complications are lower than open repair. Complex fenestrated EVAR (FEVAR) shows similar perioperative mortality to open complex repair but fewer complications and may benefit moderate- to high-risk surgical candidates.

content.narrative_summary: Common iliac artery aneurysms coexist with AAA in 20–40% of surveillance studies, and rupture at diameters <4 cm has been reported. A repair threshold of 3.5 cm is reasonable to balance procedural and rupture risks. Preservation of pelvic perfusion via at least one hypogastric artery is critical to prevent ischemic complications (buttock claudication, bowel ischemia, erectile dysfunction). Case series and retrospective analyses support aneurysm growth rates and rupture incidences, while meta-analyses demonstrate increased buttock claudication and reintervention rates when the internal iliac artery is excluded or when common iliac diameters exceed 18 mm.

rows.recommendation: For patients with asymptomatic small AAA and concomitant common iliac artery aneurysm(s) ≥3.5 cm, elective repair of both abdominal and iliac aneurysms is recommended.

When treating common iliac artery aneurysms or ectasia as part of AAA repair, preservation of at least 1 hypogastric artery is recommended, if anatomically feasible, to decrease the risk of pelvic ischemia.

content.title: Surveillance After TAA Repair
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that surveillance imaging after thoracic aneurysm repair is used to identify repair complications or monitor residual aortic pathology. CT is generally preferred, though MRI is a reasonable alternative due to avoidance of ionizing radiation and contrast allergy, despite limitations such as cost and artifact. TEVAR has higher reintervention rates and specific complications (endoleak, retrograde dissection, stent migration), while open repair is durable but carries risks of graft infection and pseudoaneurysm. Both approaches may lead to progressive dilation of adjacent segments. The supportive text details TEVAR reintervention rates, advantages and disadvantages of MRI versus CT, long-term durability and reintervention rates after open repair, and recommended surveillance intervals.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Surveillance After TAA Repair

rows.recommendation: In patients treated with TEVAR, surveillance imaging with CT is recommended after 1 month and 12 months and, if stable, annually thereafter.^1-5
In patients treated with TEVAR, longitudinal surveillance with MRI is a reasonable alternative to CT for reduction of long-term radiation exposure or avoidance of an iodinated contrast allergy.^6-9

In patients treated with open repair of the thoracic aorta without residual aortopathy, surveillance imaging with a CT or MRI within 1 year postoperatively and then every 5 years thereafter is reasonable.^10-14
In patients treated with open repair of the thoracic aorta who have residual aortopathy or abnormal findings on surveillance imaging, annual surveillance imaging is reasonable.

content.title: 6.5.6.2. Surveillance After AAA Repair
content.narrative_summary: Routine surveillance after EVAR aims to detect endoleaks, sac growth, endograft migration, or endograft failure. CT is the gold standard for follow-up imaging but exposes patients to ionizing radiation and iodinated contrast; duplex ultrasound is specific for endoleak detection but limited in assessing stent migration or noncontiguous aneurysms; MRI offers high diagnostic accuracy for endoleaks when accompanied by plain radiography. Surveillance after open AAA repair prevents late aneurysm rupture by identifying para-anastomotic and new aneurysms, with a risk of aneurysmal disease in adjacent visceral or iliac vessels and noncontiguous aortic locations.

In patients with AAA treated with EVAR who are undergoing annual surveillance imaging duplex ultrasound, additional cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis every 5 years postoperatively is reasonable.5-8
In patients with AAA treated with EVAR and abnormal findings (Table 21) on any surveillance duplex ultrasound, additional cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI is reasonable.9
In patients with AAA treated with complex EVAR, a modified surveillance imaging plan that combines cross-sectional imaging and duplex ultrasound of target vessels is reasonable.10,11
In patients with AAA who have undergone open repair, surveillance imaging with CT or MRI of the abdominopelvic aorta within 1 year postoperatively and then every 5 years thereafter is reasonable.5,6

content.title: 7.2. AAS: Diagnostic Evaluation (Imaging, Laboratory Testing)
content.narrative_summary: A plain chest x-ray is neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific for AAS diagnosis but certain radiographic findings may raise suspicion; CT, TEE, and MRI are all highly accurate, though aortography is invasive with lower sensitivity. Acute aortic dissection risk scores (eg, ADD-RS) combined with a low D-dimer may help exclude AAS in low-risk patients. No biomarkers are diagnostic. CT is widely available, rapid, and shows the full extent of dissection, branch involvement, malperfusion, and associated findings. Imaging modality choice should be individualized based on clinical presentation, specific diagnostic questions, and institutional capabilities.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for AAS: Diagnostic Evaluation (Imaging, Laboratory Testing)

content.title: Acute Medical Management of AAS
content.narrative_summary: The page reviews imaging modalities for diagnosing acute aortic syndrome (AAS), including CT, TEE/TTE, and MRI, noting their relative advantages, sensitivities, and appropriate clinical settings. A “Synopsis” emphasizes that all patients with AAS require immediate medical therapy—targeted blood pressure and heart rate control and pain management—to prevent acute and chronic complications while considering subsequent surgical or endovascular interventions.

rows.recommendation: In patients presenting to the hospital with AAS, prompt treatment with anti-impulse therapy with invasive monitoring of BP with an arterial line in an ICU setting is recommended as initial treatment to decrease aortic wall stress.
Patients with AAS should be treated to an SBP <120 mm Hg or to lowest BP that maintains adequate end-organ perfusion, as well as a target heart rate of 60 to 80 bpm.
In patients with AAS, initial management should include intravenous beta blockers, except in patients with contraindications.
In those with contraindications or intolerance to beta blockers, initial management with an intravenous non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is reasonable for heart rate control.
In patients with AAS, initial management should include intravenous vasodilators if the BP is not well controlled after initiation of intravenous beta-blocker therapy.
Patients with AAS should be treated with pain control, as needed, to help with hemodynamic management.

content.narrative_summary: The page provides an overview of acute type A aortic dissection as a life-threatening condition requiring urgent surgical evaluation due to risks of tamponade, severe aortic regurgitation, myocardial ischemia, malperfusion, and end-organ infarction. Data from IRAD (1995–2013) show surgical mortality decreased from 25% to 18% but medical mortality remained at 57%. Universal surgical risk factors include shock, tamponade, neurologic or visceral malperfusion, and preoperative myocardial ischemia. Elderly patients generally benefit from surgery, though frail patients with significant contraindications may be managed medically. Supportive text emphasizes (1) the 1% per hour mortality of unoperated acute type A dissection and the time-sensitivity of repair, (2) unpredictable risk in hemodynamically stable patients regardless of surgery timing and benefits of regionalizing care to high-volume centers, and (3) improved survival with surgery in cerebral malperfusion and stroke presentations, while noting some subsets (e.g., complete occlusion of an internal carotid artery) may not benefit.

content.title: 7.4.1.2. Management of Malperfusion
content.narrative_summary: Imaging evidence of malperfusion is present in up to 25% of patients with acute type A aortic dissection but should be distinguished from clinical malperfusion syndrome, which carries a 30.5% mortality versus 6.2% in those without syndrome. Mortality correlates with the number of branch vessels and malperfused organs. Early recognition of pulse deficits and hypotension prompts timely reperfusion, traditionally via central aortic repair at the proximal tear site. Cardiac and visceral malperfusion portend worse outcomes, leading to hybrid and endovascular-first strategies to establish end-organ perfusion before open repair. Mesenteric malperfusion has the highest mortality (63.2%), and IRAD data show a 95% in-hospital mortality when treated medically. Hybrid surgical and endovascular approaches have demonstrated lower operative mortality rates (2.1% in one series), though resource and expertise requirements limit broader application.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Malperfusion

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute type A aortic dissection presenting with renal, mesenteric, or lower extremity malperfusion, it is recommended to proceed to immediate operative repair of the ascending aorta.

In patients with acute type A aortic dissection presenting with clinically significant mesenteric (celiac, SMA) malperfusion, either immediate operative repair of the ascending aorta or immediate mesenteric revascularization via endovascular or open surgical intervention by those with this expertise before ascending aortic repair is reasonable.

content.title: 7.4.1.3. Surgical Repair Strategies in Acute Type A Aortic Dissection
section_headings: 7.4.1.3. Surgical Repair Strategies in Acute Type A Aortic Dissection
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis recommends that surgical resection for acute type A aortic dissection should include the tear site, any aneurysmal aorta, and the proximal-most extent of the dissection to reduce late complications. A nonresected primary tear increases reoperation risk. More extensive replacement involving the aortic root, arch, or both adds complexity and ischemic time but may reduce future dilation, insufficiency, or repeat dissection. Management is individualized based on pathology and patient condition; younger patients may have greater potential for late complications. Valve-sparing root replacement shows excellent outcomes but has long-term reoperative risk. Untreated aortic arch or descending thoracic tissue may undergo aneurysmal enlargement and require reintervention, particularly with acute…

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Surgical Repair Strategies in Acute Type A Aortic Dissection

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute type A aortic dissection and a partially dissected aortic root but no significant aortic valve leaflet pathology, aortic valve resuspension is recommended over valve replacement.

In patients with acute type A aortic dissection who have extensive destruction of the aortic root, a root aneurysm, or a known genetic aortic disorder, aortic root replacement is recommended with a mechanical or biologically valved conduit.
In selected patients who are stable, valve-sparing root repair may be reasonable, when performed by experienced surgeons in a Multidisciplinary Aortic Team.
In patients with acute type A aortic dissection undergoing aortic repair, an open distal anastomosis is recommended to improve survival and increase false-lumen thrombosis rates.
In patients with acute type A aortic dissection without an intimal tear in the arch or a significant arch aneurysm, hemiarch repair is recommended over more extensive arch replacement.

In patients with acute type A aortic dissection and a dissection flap extending through the arch into the descending thoracic aorta, an extended aortic repair with antegrade stenting of the proximal descending thoracic aorta may be considered to treat malperfusion and reduce late distal aortic complications.

In patients with acute type A aortic dissection undergoing surgical repair, axillary cannulation, when feasible, is reasonable over femoral cannulation to reduce the risk of stroke or retrograde malperfusion.
In patients with acute type A aortic dissection undergoing surgical repair who require circulatory arrest, cerebral perfusion is reasonable to improve neurologic outcomes.

In patients with acute type A aortic dissection undergoing surgical repair, direct aortic or innominate cannulation with imaging guidance is reasonable as an alternative to femoral or axillary cannulation.

content.narrative_summary: Aortic IMH is characterized by hemorrhage within the media of the aortic wall without intimal disruption and appears on noncontrast imaging as high-attenuation crescentic or circumferential thickening. It occurs most commonly in the descending thoracic aorta, shares classification and presenting symptoms with aortic dissection but typically affects older patients with hypertension and atherosclerosis, and less often leads to malperfusion. IMH may progress to aortic enlargement, dissection, or rupture, though hematomas can also resorb. Reported incidence varies regionally. Management strategies balance patient comorbidities, lesion location (type A vs B), and choice of medical therapy, endovascular, or open surgical repair, but prospective randomized data are limited. For IMH associated with penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer, see Section 7.6.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of IMH

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with complicated (Table 29) acute type A or type B aortic IMH, urgent repair is recommended.
2. In patients with uncomplicated acute type A IMH, prompt open surgical repair is recommended.

In selected patients with uncomplicated acute type A IMH who are at increased operative risk and do not have high-risk imaging features (Table 30), an initial or expectant approach of medical management may be considered.
3. In patients with uncomplicated acute type B IMH, medical therapy as the initial management strategy is recommended.

4. In patients with type B IMH who require repair of the distal aortic arch or descending thoracic aorta (zones 2–5) and have favorable anatomy, endovascular repair is reasonable when performed by surgeons with endovascular expertise.

5. In patients with type B IMH who require repair of the distal aortic arch or descending thoracic aorta (zones 2–5) and have unfavorable anatomy for endovascular repair, open surgical repair is reasonable.
6. In patients with uncomplicated type B IMH and high-risk imaging features (Table 30), intervention may be reasonable.

7.7.1.1 Initial Management of BTTAl in the Emergency Department
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that operative repair of penetrating aortic ulcers (PAUs) can be performed by open or endovascular techniques. Historically, open aortic replacement was standard, but contemporary series report good technical success and favorable midterm outcomes after endovascular repair in descending and infrarenal aorta. Comparative data are limited and treatment choice depends on PAU location, patient anatomy, associated pathology, and comorbidities. Endovascular approaches have lower procedure-related and in-hospital mortality, though available studies are small and potentially biased. Midterm endovascular outcomes show a 4%–8% risk of endoleak and 5% risk of new PAU formation, with similar one-year mortality compared to open repair. Open repair for ascending aortic PAU is limited to small case series and remains the gold standard for ascending arch lesions. The recommendation-specific supportive text notes that open surgery outcomes in the ascending arch inform PAU repair despite lack of FDA-approved endovascular devices for proximal arch, and that endovascular repair of descending and abdominal PAU is associated with lower early mortality but similar longer-term results.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for PAU Open Surgical Repair Versus Endovascular Repair

rows.recommendation: In patients who require repair of a PAU in the ascending aorta or proximal aortic arch (zones 0–1), open surgical repair is recommended.

In patients who require repair of a PAU in the distal aortic arch (zones 2–3), descending thoracic aorta, or abdominal aorta, either open surgical repair or endovascular repair is reasonable, based on anatomy and medical comorbidities.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that blunt thoracic aortic injury (BTTAl) is a rare but increasingly diagnosed cause of death in trauma, associated with high mortality (~19%) and requiring careful blood pressure and heart rate control. Supportive text notes the elevated risk of aortic-related mortality, the need for imaging expertise and multidisciplinary care at level I trauma centers, and the role of beta blockers and permissive hypotension, balanced against end-organ perfusion requirements in polytrauma patients.

3. In patients with grade 2 BTTAl (Figure 23) and with high-risk imaging features (Table 32), aortic intervention is reasonable.
4. In patients with grade 2 BTTAl (Figure 23) and without high-risk imaging features (Table 32), nonoperative management and follow-up surveillance imaging may be reasonable.

content.narrative_summary: The page presents narrative evidence on management and outcomes of blunt traumatic thoracic aortic injuries (BTTAl). Estrera’s original paper reported 0% mortality with grade 1 injuries managed medically. Current SVS guidelines recommend expectant management for grade 1 and repair for higher grades. Trauma studies show 32% of BTTAl managed nonoperatively with 25% mortality; overall mortality was higher in nonoperative versus operative patients (35.0% vs 11.2%), while aortic-related mortality was similar. Subsequent points note that grade 1 injuries resolve with extremely low mortality under medical management, grade 3–4 injuries carry high risk and require urgent treatment (nonoperative management alone predicted all-cause death), outcomes of grade 1–2 injuries are similar between nonoperative and TEVAR at high-volume centers, and secondary imaging signs (eg, aortic arch hematoma >15 mm) predict worse outcomes.

content.narrative_summary: Blunt aortic injuries managed nonoperatively with anti-impulse therapy and serial CTA rarely progress but can develop vessel occlusion, aneurysmal degeneration, or pseudoaneurysm requiring intervention to prevent symptomatic or life-threatening disease. Grade 4 injuries carry high risk of hypotension, aortic transection, and high early mortality despite surgical repair. Grade 2 injuries without malperfusion are often observed, but progression or malperfusion warrants endovascular or open repair; in one series, 45% were initially managed nonoperatively, 34% underwent open repair, and 21% received endovascular repair. Pseudoaneurysm repair is performed to prevent rupture, but only 30% in one multicenter study were managed nonoperatively and some failed. REBOA has reemerged for rapid hemorrhage control with improvements in SBP and survival compared to open hemorrhage control, but increased risk of acute kidney injury and limb amputation; it is contraindicated in pericardial tamponade, major thoracic hemorrhage, cardiac arrest, or shock from penetrating chest trauma.

content.narrative_summary: During pregnancy, marked aortic dilation or rapid aortic expansion increases the risk of maternal aortic dissection or rupture and may warrant pregnancy termination if early in gestation due to high maternal morbidity and mortality. Prophylactic aortic surgery during pregnancy requires individualized decision-making based on maternal and fetal risks, with first-trimester surgery carrying risks of fetal developmental defects and third-trimester surgery affecting fetal circulation and maternal hemodynamics. If type A aortic dissection occurs, urgent obstetric and cardiac surgical consultation is needed; emergency surgery before 26 weeks recognizes fetal loss risk, while after 28 weeks, cesarean delivery followed by aortic repair offers the best maternal and fetal survival. Acute type A dissections between 24–28 weeks require balancing maternal and fetal risks when choosing cesarean plus aortic surgery versus surgery with fetal monitoring. Type B dissections in pregnancy are treated medically but 20% develop complications requiring intervention, with endovascular repair preferred when feasible. Prophylactic aortic surgery remains a complex, individualized decision.

content.narrative_summary: Large-vessel vasculitis (LVV), including Takayasu arteritis and giant cell arteritis (GCA), is a common cause of aortitis alongside other etiologies such as immunoglobulin G4–related disease and relapsing polychondritis. Diagnostic criteria are summarized elsewhere (Table 35). Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent complications including aneurysm, dissection, intramural hematoma, penetrating aortic ulcer, rupture, progressive atherosclerosis, and thrombosis. 18F-FDG-PET with CT is useful both for initial diagnosis and for assessing anti-inflammatory treatment response, particularly before revascularization. Initial therapy for Takayasu arteritis and GCA typically involves high-dose glucocorticoids (prednisone 40–60 mg/d or equivalent), with adjunctive tocilizumab or methotrexate in select cases. Revascularization may be warranted in stable disease or acute aortic syndrome. Imaging of the aorta should be performed promptly as sensitivity of FDG-PET and CTA decreases after glucocorticoid initiation; FDG-PET specificity for GCA can reach 100%, and CTA sensitivity is about 85%. MRI is used in Takayasu arteritis for surveillance despite limited direct evidence. Echocardiography may aid assessment of aortic valve function when proximal involvement is confirmed by CT or MRI. Active vasculitis diagnosis relies on clinical symptoms plus biomarkers or imaging; high-dose glucocorticoids induce remission in most patients, though evidence for intravenous methylprednisolone is limited to small trials.

recommendation_tables.title: Treatment

rows.recommendation: In patients with active GCA or Takayasu arteritis, initial medical therapy should include high-dose glucocorticoids.
In patients with GCA who have evidence of active aortitis, tocilizumab is recommended as adjunctive therapy to glucocorticoids, with methotrexate as an alternative.
In all patients with Takayasu arteritis, nonbiological disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARD) should be given in combination with glucocorticoids.

In patients with active GCA or Takayasu arteritis, treatment efficacy should be periodically assessed by monitoring inflammatory serum markers (C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate), imaging with CT, MRI, or FDG-PET, and clinical symptoms.
In patients with GCA or Takayasu arteritis who are in remission, elective endovascular or open surgical intervention is reasonable to treat aortic and branch vessel complications.
In patients with GCA or Takayasu arteritis and aortic involvement who are in remission, annual surveillance imaging with CT, MRI, or FDG-PET is reasonable.

content.narrative_summary: The supportive text discusses the management of infectious aortitis or mycotic aneurysm, emphasizing prolonged antimicrobial therapy (6 weeks to 6 months) and consideration of lifelong suppressive therapy. Open surgical repair, including in situ reconstruction or extra-anatomic bypass, is often warranted given high rupture risk, though data are limited and largely from small case series. Three operative strategies are compared:
1. Extra-anatomic reconstruction: avoids foreign body in infected area; indicated for infrarenal location with gross purulence, vertebral osteomyelitis, inadequate antibiotic response, selected fistulae; disadvantages include technical infeasibility for thoracic/supra renal sites, long operating time, stump blowout, limb ischemia, higher reinfection rate, ischemic colitis.

content.title: 9.2.2. Diagnosis and Management of Prosthetic Aortic Graft Infection
section_headings: 9.2.2. Diagnosis and Management of Prosthetic Aortic Graft Infection
content.narrative_summary: The page opens mid-discussion noting that antimicrobial therapy alone without surgical intervention is associated with high mortality and does not prevent aneurysm expansion or rupture, and is therefore reserved for patients not candidates for repair or those receiving palliative care. Expert opinion suggests at least 6 weeks of therapy, possibly longer. The response of uncomplicated infectious aortitis to antimicrobial therapy may influence the choice and timing of interventional approaches, and surveillance imaging by a multidisciplinary team is reasonable. The Synopsis clarifies that these recommendations apply to prosthetic aortic grafts, including tube grafts via open or endovascular approaches, as well as allografts and autografts, and notes that aortic graft infection is uncommon (0.3%–3%), with increased risk when involving the groin; common sources include contamination at implantation and enteric erosion or fistula formation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnosis and Management of Prosthetic Aortic Graft Infection

rows.recommendation: In patients with a prosthetic aortic graft, who have signs and symptoms or culture evidence of unexplained infection or have unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding, cross-sectional imaging is reasonable to evaluate for an underlying aortic graft infection.1-6

In patients with an infected prosthetic aortic graft who are hemodynamically stable and have appropriate anatomy, it is reasonable to perform open surgery with either in situ reconstruction or extra-anatomic bypass.7-13
In patients with an infected prosthetic aortic graft who are hemodynamically unstable, it is reasonable to perform open surgery with either explant or in situ reconstruction.7

In patients with an infected prosthetic aortic graft, endovascular therapy is reasonable, either as bridge therapy in those with hemodynamic instability or as long-term therapy in those who are unsuitable candidates for open surgery.13-15

In patients who have undergone treatment of an acute prosthetic aortic graft infection, targeted intravenous antimicrobial therapy of at least 6 weeks’ duration, with prolonged suppressive oral therapy in select cases, plus a consultation and follow-up with an infectious disease specialist, is recommended.7,11,12,16,17

In patients with an infected prosthetic aortic graft and either an extensive perigraft abscess or an infection caused by methicillin-resistant S. aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or a multidrug-resistant microorganism, or who have undergone in situ reconstruction, lifelong suppressive oral antimicrobial therapy may be considered after the initial course of therapy.14,15,18,19

content.title: 9.3. Atherosclerotic Disease
content.narrative_summary: Atherosclerosis is a chronic immunoinflammatory, fibroproliferative disease of the aorta and its branches propagated by lipids, beginning early in life and often diagnosed incidentally during evaluation of vascular events. Management includes control of risk factors, lifestyle modification, and pharmacological therapies tailored to concomitant conditions such as coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, and PAD. Although lifestyle changes are vital, compliance can be challenging.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Atherosclerotic Disease

rows.recommendation: In patients with aortic atherosclerotic disease and concomitant coronary artery disease, PAD or both, it is recommended to prescribe antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulant therapy or both, guided by the clinical setting.
In patients with aortic atherosclerotic disease and risk factors for confirmed coronary artery disease, it is reasonable to prescribe a moderate- or high-intensity statin.
In patients with aortic atheromas of a thickness ≥4 mm, statin therapy may be reasonable.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of coarctation of the aorta (CoA), noting that transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is useful for assessing the CoA gradient and identifying coexisting bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) in about 50% of patients. Untreated CoA may lead to aortic dissection, heart failure, cerebral aneurysm, hypoperfusion, and hypertension. Late complications after surgical or endovascular repair include graft undersizing, restenosis, aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm formation, rupture, and persistent hypertension. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and exercise testing aid diagnosis and management, and lifelong imaging follow-up is recommended. An aberrant subclavian artery (ASCA) may be incidentally found but can cause dysphagia, dyspnea, aneurysm, or Kommerell diverticulum, which may require treatment if symptomatic or large. The Synopsis reiterates anatomic variants, associated BAV, intracranial and ascending aneurysms, complications of untreated CoA, repair options, late complications, and the need for long-term follow-up.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for CoA

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with CoA, including those who have undergone surgical or endovascular intervention, an MRI or CT is recommended for initial, surveillance, and follow-up aortic imaging.1-4
2. In patients with CoA, BPs should be measured in both arms and one of the lower extremities.
3. In patients with significant native or recurrent CoA (Table 37) and hypertension, endovascular stenting or open surgical repair of the coarctation is recommended.2,3,5-12
4. In patients with CoA, guideline-directed medical therapy is recommended for the treatment of hypertension.13
5. In adult patients with CoA, screening for intracranial aneurysms by MRI or CT may be reasonable.14-18

section_headings: 10. PHYSICAL ACTIVITY AND QUALITY OF LIFE
content.narrative_summary: This page introduces the importance of physical activity and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in patients with aortic disease. The synopsis discusses the growing focus on patient-reported HRQOL measures (eg, SF-36 and aneurysm-specific tools), factors affecting HRQOL including postoperative recovery and socioeconomic influences, and the need for standardized preoperative and postoperative HRQOL reporting. It notes that patients with adequately controlled aortic aneurysms may benefit from moderate-intensity aerobic activity, while the effects of resistance training on aortic blood pressure and aneurysm progression require further study. The recommendation-specific supportive text emphasizes limited data on safe exercise forms, the physiologic benefits and hemodynamic consequences of exertion, and a consensus to avoid intense isometric exertion requiring the Valsalva maneuver.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Physical Activity and Quality of Life

rows.recommendation: 1. For patients with significant aortic disease, education and guidance should be provided about avoiding intense isometric exercises (eg, heavy weightlifting or activities requiring the Valsalva maneuver), burst exertion and activities, and collision sports.1,2
2. For patients who have undergone surgery for aortic aneurysm or dissection, postoperative cardiac rehabilitation is recommended.3,4

3. In patients with thoracic or abdominal aortic aneurysms whose BP is adequately controlled, it is reasonable to encourage 30 to 60 minutes of mild-to-moderate intensity aerobic activity at least 3 to 4 days per week.5,6

4. For patients with clinically significant aortic disease, it is reasonable to screen for anxiety, depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder and, when indicated, provide resources for support7,8; it is also reasonable to provide education and resources to minimize patients' concerns, support optimal decision-making, and enhance quality of life.5,9-11

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of exercise in patients with aortic disease, noting that exercise intensity should be individualized based on factors such as aortic pathology, diameter, aortic size index, family history, and hypertension. Cardiac rehabilitation post-aortic surgery appears safe and beneficial, improving peak oxygen uptake and HRQOL, while moderate-intensity exercise may be cardioprotective. section_headings: 12.5. Quality of Life in Patients With Aortic Disease
content.narrative_summary: Section 12.5 highlights a lack of baseline HRQOL data in aortic disease patients, limited studies on physical, mental, emotional, sexual, and professional outcomes after endovascular or open repair, scarce evidence for hereditary thoracic aortic aneurysm conditions beyond Marfan syndrome, and a need for research to improve engagement among disadvantaged or lower‐educated patients. Section 12.7 notes very limited research on optimal exercise and rehabilitation strategies for patients with aortic disease, particularly for those with untreated diseased segments or who do not meet surgical thresholds, and calls for patient‐centric rehabilitation protocols. Section 12.8 discusses sociodemographic disparities, market factors affecting cardiovascular and aortic care decision‐making, and the need for regional quality improvement, standardized practice, physician participation, and educational interventions to improve awareness and care in underserved areas.
